newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon holds parliamentary elections for Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Gabon holds parliamentary elections for Sunday.

text.p: Gabon holds the first round of its much-delayed parliamentary elections on Sunday, with the opposition saying it is determined to take part despite delays in issuing voter cards and posting of electoral lists.

"We are ready. We will take part in the elections if they are held tomorrow, the day after, tonight, with or without electoral lists and voter cards," Father Paul Mba Abessole of the main opposition National Woodcutter's Rally (RNB) said.

Sunday's elections, which follow chaotic local elections in October, are part of a timetable of democratic and electoral reforms brokered in Paris after violence marred President Omar Bongo's 1993 relection.
The date of the poll in the forested equatorial oil producer country, initially planned for December 1, was not announced until Monday. A second round is scheduled for December 29.

Opposition parties have described the way the elections were called as unlawful and have denounced delays in the issuing of voter cards and the fact that electoral lists in certain opposition strongholds only were processed in France.
Under the electoral law, voter cards must be distributed and electoral lists displayed eight days before polling.
Electoral material was still being flown to the interior of the country on Friday.
The head of the electoral commission, citing organisational problems, postponed the election indefinitely on November 30, less than 24 hours before voters were to go to the polls.
At the time, Antoine Nguema Essone cited problems stemming from chaotic local elections on October 20, in particular names disappearing from voter lists.
The government approved the new date on Monday.
Gabon, a former French colony of just 1.2 million people, has an electorate of about 500,000.

Sunday's vote will be Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa's after the fall of Communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.
More than 1,000 candidates will be bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly on Sunday.
Bongo has ruled the former French colony since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba.
His Democratic Party is expected to face strong competition from the Woodcutters Rally, led by Abessole, a Roman Catholic priest and runner-up to Bongo in 1993.

That election triggered opposition protests in which at least five people died. Pay protests turned violent and political in early 1994. The official death toll was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
The Woodcutters won the capital Libreville during October's municipal polls and Abessole is likely to become the capital's future mayor. City councillors have yet to vote.
Polls open at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) on Sunday and close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT). Based on previous experience, results could take over a week to trickle out.
